design_detail: Investigator-initiated, open-label, single-group phase 2 proof-of-principle trial (EudraCT 2021-000805-26; protocol published as Kvam et al., 2022) at Østfold Hospital Trust, Norway, recruiting January 2023 to May 2024: 12 adults with moderate to severe major depressive disorder received three 90-minute preparatory sessions, two all-day MDMA sessions about 4 weeks apart with an overnight stay, telephone follow-up and three 90-minute integration sessions after each, with an inner-directed MDMA-assisted therapy approach; primary outcome the change in clinician-rated MADRS from baseline to about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session (about 12 weeks after baseline), secondary the Sheehan Disability Scale. A corrigendum (Kvam et al., 2026; card sc_kvam_2026a) corrects one participant's post-treatment MADRS score; this card gives the corrected values. Funded by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority; Lykos Therapeutics provided the MDMA and an unconditional grant. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I.
can_establish: That two open-label MDMA sessions within a structured psychotherapy programme could be given to 12 people with major depressive disorder without dropouts or serious adverse events, and how far their clinician-rated depression and functional impairment fell over about 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, the eleven or so psychotherapy sessions, expectation (participants were almost all self-referred), regression to the mean (entry required a MADRS of at least 20 at baseline) or natural fluctuation produced the fall (no control group, raters not blind); whether improvement lasts (reported separately at 7 months); rare harms; or effects in people with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, personality disorders, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk or cardiovascular risk, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Self-referrals and referrals from general practitioners, psychiatrists or psychotherapists; 11 of the 12 self-referred and 1 was referred by a study therapist; no referral from other professionals was eligible (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph). Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 86 telephone-screened, 65 excluded after telephone screening, 21 screened, 6 screening failures, 15 enrolled, 3 early terminations before dosing, 12 completed dosing session 1 and the primary end point.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: DSM-5 major depressive disorder, single or recurrent, without psychotic features, current episode longer than 12 weeks and shorter than 2 years; MADRS of 20 or more at enrolment and again at the baseline visit (V3); age 18 or older. Excluded: psychotic disorders, mania, personality disorders, eating disorders with purging, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk, pregnancy, recent electroconvulsive therapy or ketamine, and medical conditions made risky by raised blood pressure or heart rate (Method › Participants, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Procedures, 2nd paragraph). The EU register adds the exclusion of people who had used ecstasy more than 10 times in 10 years or at all within 6 months of the first session, or had been in a MAPS-sponsored MDMA trial (registry record).
sample.demographics: 7 women and 5 men; mean age 44.1 (SD 9.2); 11 White, 1 Asian; 2 of non-Norwegian origin; mean 18.6 years of education; 11 with recurrent MDD, mean 16.1 years (10.4) since the first episode; baseline MADRS 29.6 (4.9), 10 moderate and 2 severe; comorbid PTSD 3 (25.0%) and ADHD 3 (25.0%); previous antidepressants 9 (75.0%), 8 tapering ongoing psychotropic medicines; previous psychological treatments 5.5 courses (3.3) and 223.1 sessions (333.9; median 88.5); 7 on sick leave in the past 3 months; previous MDMA use 1 (8.3%) (Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Three of 15 enrolled stopped before dosing (reasons not given in this paper, which refers to the protocol article); no early terminations, dropouts or losses after dosing; all 12 dosed reached the primary end point (Fig. 1; Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Almost all self-referred, highly educated and with long histories of psychotherapy; the authors note that self-referral may have raised expectations and exaggerated the pre–post differences (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Analysis is of the 12 who were dosed, not the 15 enrolled.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: three 90-minute preparatory sessions and a baseline visit; psychotropic medicines tapered after enrolment; two MDMA sessions about 4 weeks apart, each about 8 hours with a pair of therapists, ended by a study physician's assessment, with an overnight stay; four telephone calls in the following week and three 90-minute integration sessions over the next 4 weeks; therapists were three psychologists and a psychiatrist (three trained for a sponsored PTSD trial); adherence to the therapy manual was not rated (Method › Procedures, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: first session an initial dose of 80 mg MDMA, second session 120 mg (all participants accepted the increase), each with a supplemental half of the initial dose offered 90 to 120 minutes later; all but one participant took the supplement in both sessions (Method › Procedures, 3rd paragraph). The route is not stated in this paper.
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorders were excluded; AUDIT and DUDIT did not change (3.3 to 3.3; 0.6 to 0.1); no adverse events related to MDMA use outside the study were reported (Table 2; Results › Safety, 6th paragraph). During the treatment period six participants took psychotropic medicines for other conditions (two resumed lisdexamfetamine; others hydroxyzine, zopiclone, alimemazine or oxazepam; one codeine for a rib fracture), and two received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for adverse events (Results › Safety, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; ongoing psychotropic medicines were tapered after enrolment in 8 of 12 (Table 1).

comparison.controls: None: change from the baseline visit to the outcome visit about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; the authors state that without a control group they cannot tell whether the response was due to the treatment, expectancy or natural fluctuation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: MADRS (clinician-rated). Secondary: Sheehan Disability Scale (SDS). Exploratory: BDI-II, Bergen Insomnia Scale, PCL-5, GAD-7, AUDIT, DUDIT; responders (MADRS reduction of 50% or more) and remitters (MADRS 12 or less). Safety: adverse events recorded by the therapists with the sub-investigator; treatment-emergent adverse events and psychotropic co-medication during and for 2 days after dosing and through treatment; C-SSRS, any deterioration from baseline being recorded as an adverse event; adverse events of special interest (cardiac, serious suicidal ideation or behaviour, abuse potential); blood pressure, heart rate and temperature before each dose and at the end of sessions (Method › Outcome measures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. MADRS raters were affiliated with the hospital but not the study team; not fully blinded, though said to be largely unaware whether an assessment was before or after treatment (Method › Procedures, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Mean change from baseline to the outcome visit, tested with the two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with 95% CIs from 4,000 bootstrap resamples of the mean change; a mixed-effects model for repeated BDI-II (Method › Statistics, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten pre–post tests in Table 2 (MADRS, SDS total and two SDS items, BDI-II, GAD-7, PCL-5, BIS, AUDIT, DUDIT) plus the BDI-II mixed model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Open label. The authors say raters were neither completely independent nor blinded, so rater bias may have inflated the MADRS change; adverse events were reported to the therapy team, which may have led to under-reporting (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Corrected values (corrigendum): MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3; s.e. 2.4), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, z = −3.06, P < 0.001 (the original article printed the outcome as 9.7, SD 10.0). Among the 9 without comorbid PTSD, mean change −18.1 (8.8). SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2), change −11.7 (SD 7.6), CI −7.6 to −15.8, P = 0.001. Responders 9 of 12 (75.0%) and remitters 9 of 12 (75.0%). Exploratory: BDI-II 33.5 to 12.0 (−21.5; −14.0 to −29.0); GAD-7 13.8 to 6.0 (printed difference −9.0); PCL-5 36.4 to 25.4 (−11.0; −2.4 to −19.6); BIS 28.9 to 12.6 (−16.3); BDI-II mixed model −0.19 points per day (95% CI −0.24 to −0.15) (Results › Primary outcome; Secondary outcome; Exploratory analysis; Table 2; corrigendum). Within-group changes only; no comparison exists.
analysis.preregistration_detail: EU Clinical Trials Register, EudraCT 2021-000805-26: record first entered 4 August 2021, ethics opinion 25 June 2021, competent authority decision 19 November 2021, before recruitment (January 2023); an open-label phase 2 feasibility study sponsored by Østfold Hospital Trust; main objective the mean change in MADRS from visit 4 (baseline) to visit 13 (about 12 weeks after baseline); secondary endpoint feasibility measured by a 15-item subjective-effects visual analogue scale; status ongoing, no results posted (registry record, read on clinicaltrialsregister.eu on 2026-10-17). The article reports SDS as its secondary outcome and does not report the registered subjective-effects scale; it takes baseline MADRS at visit 3; it calls safety and feasibility the primary objectives. The protocol article (2022) was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse-event lists, vital signs and suicidal-ideation trajectories are only in the supplementary files (PDF, Word and PowerPoint downloads), not read; the registered subjective-effects endpoint is not reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a proof-of-principle sample of 12.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 people with moderate to severe, mostly recurrent depression, clinician-rated depression fell from about 30 to about 10 on the MADRS some 8 weeks after the second of two open-label MDMA sessions within an intensive psychotherapy programme; 9 of 12 met both response and remission thresholds and functional impairment fell. No one dropped out after dosing and there were no serious adverse events, but six participants had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation recorded as adverse events and two needed benzodiazepines and zopiclone after dosing. There is no comparison group, the raters knew everyone had been treated, and expectations were probably high, so none of the change can be attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the study provided "indications of efficacy" (Abstract › Conclusion). The Discussion says the authors demonstrated that MDMA-assisted therapy can be safely administered to people with major depressive disorder (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and compares the 9 of 12 responders and remitters with the loss of PTSD diagnosis in 67% and 71% of the MDMA arms of the two phase 3 trials (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), a comparison across designs, outcomes and populations; it attributes part of the improvement to participants' work on traumatic material, which is not tested (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The Limitations state that without a control group the response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than to expectancy or natural fluctuation, and that the trial cannot draw conclusions about efficacy (Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Kvam et al., Front Psychiatry: the study protocol (on the project's evidence map; not read here).
Kvam et al., Br J Psychiatry: corrigendum correcting one participant's post-treatment MADRS score (card sc_kvam_2026a).
Kvam et al., J Psychiatr Res: seven-month follow-up of the same 12 participants (on ScienceDirect, not readable in this session; not read).
Ai et al. and Kvam et al., Br J Psychiatry: a commentary on this trial and the authors' reply (on the project's evidence map; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: One open-label trial of 12 people, from one team; no randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for depression is among the sources read. The authors call for randomized trials.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated; funded by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority (project 2021007); Lykos Therapeutics provided the study drug and an unconditional grant (Funding). The protocol was written with a template from Lykos Therapeutics, and two authors secured the agreement with Lykos (Author contributions).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: MDMA was provided by Lykos Therapeutics; T.-M.K. received a lecture honorarium from Lundbeck; L.H.S. is employed by Axon Clinic; O.A.A. is a consultant for Cortechs.ai and has received speaker honoraria from Janssen, Lilly, Lundbeck and Sunovion; I.W.G. runs an online training programme in MDMA-assisted therapy through his clinic Psykologvirke; several authors at Østfold Hospital (T.-M.K., I.W.G., L.H.S., O.A.A.) received research support from Lykos Therapeutics for an MDMA-assisted therapy trial for PTSD (Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The first author and two other authors were study therapists (Author contributions); one author sells training in the therapy. The authors used ChatGPT to improve parts of the text (Acknowledgements). Data available on reasonable request (Data availability).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in major depressive disorder comparing the same psychotherapy with MDMA against an active placebo, with blinded independent raters, measured expectancy, an independent adverse-event assessor and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group. The package includes about eleven psychotherapy sessions, itself an effective treatment for depression; entry required a MADRS of 20 or more at baseline, inviting regression to the mean; expectations were probably high. MDMA's contribution cannot be estimated.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Eleven of 12 self-referred and one referred by a study therapist; the analysis covers the 12 dosed, not the 15 enrolled (3 stopped before dosing).
Same protocol for all; all accepted the second-session increase and all but one took the supplements.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Six participants took psychotropic medicines for other conditions during treatment, two received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for adverse events, three needed seven extra visits, and adherence to the manual was not assessed.
All 12 dosed participants reached the primary end point.

MADRS raters were not blind and not fully independent, as the authors state; secondary and exploratory outcomes are self-reports by people who knew they had taken MDMA; adverse events were recorded by the therapists.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Prospectively registered with the MADRS change as the main objective, but the registered secondary endpoint (a subjective-effects scale) is replaced by the SDS, and one primary-outcome value had to be corrected after publication.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence of the effect of MDMA-assisted therapy on depression the study is at critical risk of bias: it has no comparison group, the treatment includes substantial psychotherapy, and enrolment at a high score invites regression to the mean; unblinded rating adds a serious concern that the authors acknowledge. The paper can be cited for feasibility (no dropouts after dosing), for the observed fall in MADRS in 12 people, and for the adverse events recorded, including worsening suicidal ideation in some participants; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for comparison with other treatments, or for durability.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 86 telephone-screened, 65 excluded, 21 screened, 6 screening failures, 15 enrolled, 3 early terminations before dosing, 12 dosed, none lost afterwards; 12 reached the primary end point. Recruitment January 2023 to May 2024; 11 self-referred, 1 referred by a study therapist.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline: 7 women and 5 men, mean age 44.1 (SD 9.2); 11 White; 11 with recurrent MDD; mean 16.1 years since the first episode; MADRS 29.6 (4.9), 10 moderate and 2 severe; comorbid PTSD 3 and ADHD 3; previous antidepressants 9 (75.0%); 8 tapered ongoing psychotropic medicines; mean 223.1 previous psychotherapy sessions (median 88.5); SDS 21.3 (6.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, corrected: MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, Wilcoxon z = −3.06, P < 0.001. Among the 9 participants without comorbid PTSD the mean change was −18.1 (8.8).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (MADRS row); corrigendum (PMC13051208), corrected Table 2
key_findings.note: The original article printed the outcome mean as 9.7 (SD 10.0), which did not match the printed change (29.6 − 9.7 = 19.9); the corrigendum's 10.3 does. The abstract gives the interval as −14.8 to −23.8.

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcome: SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2); mean change −11.7 (SD 7.6), 95% CI −7.6 to −15.8, z = −3.02, P = 0.001.
Responders (MADRS reduction of 50% or more): 9 of 12 (75.0%); remitters (MADRS 12 or less): 9 of 12 (75.0%); the corrigendum says these counts are unaffected by the correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory analysis, 1st paragraph; corrigendum, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory outcomes, baseline to the termination visit: BDI-II 33.5 (9.6) to 12.0 (14.8), −21.5 (−14.0 to −29.0); GAD-7 13.8 (4.2) to 6.0 (5.4), printed difference −9.0 (−6.0 to −12.0); PCL-5 36.4 (17.0) to 25.4 (19.7), −11.0 (−2.4 to −19.6); Bergen Insomnia Scale 28.9 (7.5) to 12.6 (10.5), −16.3; AUDIT 3.3 to 3.3 and DUDIT 0.6 to 0.1, no significant change.

Adverse events: 10 of 12 had at least one; 46 events, 45 treatment-emergent (one, a deterioration in suicidal ideation, occurred before the study drug); 15 moderate and 31 mild; no serious or severe adverse events, no adverse events of special interest, no discontinuations or hospitalisations; most common were headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; the 3 non-responders had 25 events (13 moderate) and the 9 responders 21 (2 moderate); 39 of 46 resolved within a week (mean duration 7.3 days, SD 17.6, median 1.0).

Adverse events needing treatment: ten needed psychotherapeutic support at scheduled visits; three participants needed seven extra visits; two participants received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for anxiety and insomnia within 2 days after dosing (one also a benzodiazepine later); paracetamol for eight headaches.

Suicidality: no serious suicidal ideation (C-SSRS 4 or 5) and no suicidal behaviour; one participant's ideation score increased over the study; six participants (12 adverse events) had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation; no ideation was reported during dosing sessions; group means never exceeded the 6-month baseline measured at screening.

No cardiovascular adverse events or arrhythmias; transient rises in blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature during sessions (values only in Supplementary Fig. 5, not read); no adverse events related to MDMA use outside the study.

Limitations stated by the authors: no control group, so response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than expectancy or natural fluctuation; raters neither completely independent nor blinded, so rater bias may have inflated the MADRS change; adverse events reported to the therapy team, so possibly under-reported; adherence to the manual not assessed; a self-referred sample with possibly elevated expectations.

Registration: EudraCT 2021-000805-26, first entered 4 August 2021; open-label phase 2 feasibility study; main objective the mean change in MADRS from visit 4 (baseline) to visit 13 (about 12 weeks); secondary endpoint feasibility measured by a 15-item subjective-effects visual analogue scale; ongoing, no results posted.
key_findings.locator: EU Clinical Trials Register, trial 2021-000805-26 (NO) › A. Protocol information; E.2 Objectives; E.5 End points

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority; Lykos Therapeutics provided the MDMA and an unconditional grant, and the protocol used a Lykos template; four authors received Lykos research support for a PTSD trial; one runs a training programme in MDMA-assisted therapy.

reporting_issues.issue: As first published, the MADRS outcome mean (9.7, SD 10.0) did not match the printed change (−19.3 from a baseline of 29.6); the corrigendum replaces it with 10.3 (8.3), which does, and leaves the change, its interval and the test unchanged.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2); corrigendum PMC13051208
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the corrected values; the article's own text in PMC still shows the uncorrected ones.

reporting_issues.issue: Other rows of Table 2 still do not add up, in the original and in the corrected table: GAD-7 13.8 to 6.0 is a fall of 7.8, printed as −9.0; SDS days lost 2.5 to 1.0 is 1.5, printed as −2.0; SDS underproductive days 6.1 to 2.4 is 3.7, printed as −4.1. The corrigendum does not mention them.
reporting_issues.consequence: These exploratory differences cannot be verified from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Suicidal-ideation adverse events are counted inconsistently: the Results say six participants (12 events) had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation, and any C-SSRS deterioration was to be recorded as an adverse event, while the Discussion gives the frequency of suicidal ideation as 33.3% (4 of 12) when comparing with MAPP1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Method › Outcome measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Safety, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of participants with worsening suicidal ideation may be 4 or 6 of 12; the comparison with MAPP1 rests on the lower figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the MADRS interval as −14.8 to −23.8 and the SDS interval as −7.5 to −15.9; the Results and Table 2 give −14.9 to −23.7 and −7.6 to −15.8 (the Results print the SDS interval without signs).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Results › Primary and Secondary outcome; Table 2)

reporting_issues.issue: The registered secondary endpoint (feasibility measured by a subjective-effects scale) is not reported; the article reports the SDS as its secondary outcome and names safety and feasibility as its primary objectives, while the register's main objective is the MADRS effect; baseline is visit 3 in the article and visit 4 in the register.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (E.2, E.5); PMC HTML (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Method › Outcome measures, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 footnote b)
reporting_issues.consequence: Secondary outcome switching; the primary outcome is as registered.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the MDMA-assisted therapy model (two or three monthly 8-hour sessions with preparatory and integrative sessions) citing the pooled phase 2 analysis (Mithoefer et al., 2019; reference 12), which PMC's reference list marks as retracted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background only; nothing on this card rests on it (METHODS §3.2).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12550655 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, the Fig. 1 CONSORT image viewed at its PMC address, funding, interests, contributions), read in this reader's own browser tab, with its corrigendum PMC13051208 read the same day; EU Clinical Trials Register record 2021-000805-26 (Norwegian protocol page) for registration and endpoints; the Crossref records of both DOIs. Supplementary materials 1 to 11 (PDF, Word and PowerPoint files) were not read because they are downloads; Fig. 2 values were not extracted.
